title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Appropriate Equipment & Instrumentation - Biotechnology - Graduated cylinders, serological pipettes
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: When utilizing a sterile $10 \text{ mL}$ serological pipette and a motorized pipette controller to transfer mammalian cell culture media, which of the following operational practices ensures the media remains uncontaminated and the controller functions properly?
options: Drawing the liquid up extremely rapidly until it deliberately saturates the cotton plug at the top of the pipette.
Keeping the pipette in a perfectly vertical orientation and ensuring the liquid never touches the internal cotton filter plug.
Removing the cotton plug with sterile forceps prior to the draw to prevent air bubbles from forming in the media.
Inverting the pipette completely once filled to thoroughly mix the media before dispensing.
questions.explain:
Serological pipettes are equipped with a cotton filter plug at the top specifically to act as a barrier, preventing aerosols or fluid from entering and destroying the motorized pipette controller. 

If the technician allows liquid to rise too high and wet the cotton plug (Option 'a'), the filter is ruined, liquid is pulled into the motorized pump (causing cross-contamination and mechanical failure), and the pipette itself loses accurate calibration. The device must be held vertically (Option 'b') to safely control the meniscus and avoid splashing the filter.

questions.q: A technician is dispensing $5.0 \text{ mL}$ of an enzyme reagent using a glass serological pipette that features two prominent frosted rings etched near the mouthpiece. What do these specific etched rings indicate regarding the required dispensing technique?
options: The pipette is classified "To Contain" (TC) and must be rigorously rinsed with solvent to yield the true volume.
It is a "blow-out" pipette, meaning the remaining drop of liquid in the tip must be forcefully expelled to deliver the full calibrated volume.
The pipette is constructed from heat-tempered borosilicate glass and is safe for direct open-flame sterilization.
The liquid must be allowed to drain exclusively by natural gravity without any applied air pressure.
questions.explain:
Volumetric glassware uses standardized visual cues. 

One or two **frosted (or etched) bands** near the upper end of a serological pipette indicate that it is a **"blow-out" pipette** (often marked "To Deliver" or TD). Because the volume graduations run all the way down to the very tip, simply letting gravity drain the liquid will leave a final unmeasured drop trapped by capillary action. The technician must use a bulb or motorized controller to push a final blast of air through the tip to "blow out" that last drop to achieve the true $5.0 \text{ mL}$ volume.

questions.q: A laboratory technician must prepare exactly $1.00 \text{ Liter}$ of a highly accurate $1\times$ Phosphate Buffered Saline (PBS) solution from a solid powder. To dissolve the powder and bring the total final volume to exactly $1000 \text{ mL}$ with the highest degree of quantitative precision, which piece of glassware is uniquely engineered for this specific task?
questions.explain:
A **volumetric flask** features a wide base for mixing and a highly narrowed, elongated neck with a single precisely etched calibration mark. 

Because the neck is so narrow, the meniscus is extremely distinct, allowing for an incredibly precise measurement of a single specified volume (e.g., $1000 \text{ mL}$). Beakers and Erlenmeyer flasks (Options 'a' and 'b') are meant for mixing or boiling, and their markings are only estimates (usually $\pm 5\%$ error). Graduated cylinders (Option 'd') are accurate for transferring varying amounts of liquid, but not as highly calibrated as a volumetric flask for making standard solutions.
